title: Nonlinear Interaction and Topological Selection Rules in two Skyrmion Merging: Emergence of Skyrmionium Textures
summary: The nonlinear interaction of closely spaced magnetic skyrmions remains poorly understood, particularly the conditions governing their merger into a single skyrmion or a stable skyrmionium. Here, we investigate the merging dynamics of two Néel skyrmions using analytical modelling and micromagnetic simulations based on Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics. We examine the effects of exchange, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, anisotropy, and magnetostatic energies by varying the initial separation, polarity, winding number, and skyrmion size. Our results reveal a topological selection rule: skyrmions with identical polarity and opposite winding numbers form a stable skyrmionium at intermediate overlap, while all other configurations relax into a single skyrmion. We also identify a critical radius below which the skyrmionium collapses, showing that its formation requires both the appropriate topology and a minimum size. Energy analysis reveals that the transition involves cooperative relaxation of exchange frustration and redistribution of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and magnetostatic energies, leading to a double-domain-wall structure. The resulting skyrmionium exhibits persistent breathing oscillations around an equilibrium radius, confirming its dynamical stability as a metastable state. These findings establish a predictive framework for controlling skyrmion merging and provide design guidelines for engineering skyrmionium textures in chiral magnetic nanostructures.

title: Ground-state properties of uniaxial magnetic model for antiferromagnetic 1/1 periodic approximants to icosahedral quasicrystals
summary: The ground-state properties of the uniaxial magnetic model in the 1/1 periodic approximant to the icosahedral quasicrystal with antiferromagnetic interactions for the nearest-neighbor bond $J_1$ and the next-nearest-neighbor bond $J_2$ are analyzed theoretically. By performing numerically-exact calculation, we have determined the ground-state phase diagram for the interaction strength $J_2/J_1$ and the magnetic anisotropy defined within the mirror plane reflecting the effect of the crystalline electric field. We have discovered non-collinear magnetic structures, whose magnetic space groups are identified as the antiferromagnetic orders $I_{\rm P}m'\bar{3}'$ and $R_{\rm R}\bar{3}$ with the magnetic propagation vector $(111)$ as well as the antiferromagnetic orders $Im'm'm'$ and $R\bar{3}'$ with the magnetic propagation vector $(000)$ and the ferrimagnetic orders $Im'm'2$, $I2'2'2$, $P2'/m'$, and $P\bar{1}$. By analyzing each ground state with degeneracy, we have revealed the magnetic as well as topological properties, which are useful to analyze experimental observations of rare-earth-based 1/1 approximants considering the effect of magnetic domains.

title: Quantum Noise Engineering in Advanced LIGO
comment: Submitted to Contemporary Physics. Open source tools developed for this manuscript can be found in: https://github.com/BKabagoz/LIGO-quantum-tools
summary: Advanced LIGO is a gravitational-wave detector with extreme sensitivity, operating close to the quantum limits of optical measurement. The quantum noise in this system arises from vacuum fluctuations entering the interferometer readout port: phase-like fluctuations produce measurement imprecision, while amplitude-like fluctuations drive radiation-pressure back-action. In this review, we present an intuitive description in terms of complex fields and quadratures, and follow squeezed vacuum from its generation, through its interaction with the filter cavity and propagation through the interferometer, to the readout. We discuss how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer quantum noise, and how correlations between optical quadratures map onto correlations between measurement imprecision and back-action. We conclude that LIGO is both a gravitational-wave observatory and a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.

title: Thermally-driven quantum reservoir computing
summary: Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

title: Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation
summary: Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as $L^{-1/2}$ with chain length $L$ only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.

title: Signature of chiral anomaly in a graphene-based heterostructure
summary: Chiral anomaly is a fundamental manifestation of topological matter caused by chirality imbalance. It can be of great practical value by providing a mechanism for dissipationless transport. The phenomenon is highly sensitive to the system dimensionality, disappearing in the 2D limit. Different schemes have been proposed to observe the chiral anomaly in graphene-based systems but experimental evidence has been lacking. Here, we synthesized two types of the Gr/Sr/SiC nanostructure - with 2D and 3D, bulk-like, layers of Sr - the difference being the amount of Sr intercalated under graphene. In contrast to the 2D material, 3D Gr/Sr/SiC exhibits a signature of the chiral anomaly - quadratic negative magnetoresistance in parallel magnetic and electric fields. Also, the functional form of the temperature dependence of the magnetoresistance agrees with the chiral anomaly. In addition, the 3D heterostructure exhibits suppressed conductivity and quantum oscillations in graphene. These effects may be associated with the graphene layer incorporated into a complex 3D heterostructure. Hopefully, the discovered signature of chiral anomaly in the built-in graphene would spur research on the phenomenon in topological nanomaterials.

title: Photoinduced switching of orbital-selective Mott states
summary: We investigate light-driven inversion of orbital selectivity in a two-orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model initially in an orbital-selective Mott phase. Using the matrix-product-state we show that tailored pulse excitations drive interorbital charge transfer that nearly reverses the orbital occupations. Single-particle spectral snapshots exhibit changes consistent with an interchange of the localized and itinerant characters of the orbitals. We analyze the relevant one- and two-photon excitation channels and show that chirping around the lower-frequency resonance enhances the transfer. These results establish a microscopic route to reversing orbital selectivity and accessing long-lived nonequilibrium states in multiorbital systems.

title: Particle-loss error correction using $2^l$-step states generated via particle-number-resolving measurement schemes
summary: We present an iterative scheme for generating finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by $2^l$ ($2^l$-step states). We derive an upper bound on the probability of generating such states. Based on the proposed class of states, we construct several bosonic encodings and compare their performance in correcting particle-loss errors. Our results identify the most efficient encoding, which achieves a higher channel fidelity than previously studied bosonic encodings.

title: On the critical value of void percolation in high dimensions
summary: In the random Lorentz gas, a point tracer moves through spherical obstacles of (reduced) density $Φ$ centered on a Poisson point process in $d$-dimensional space, $\mathbb{R}^d$, and becomes localized once the vacant space stops percolating, at $Φ_{\rm p}(d)$. The dimensional scaling of this void percolation threshold has remained elusive. Prior bounds, conjectural ones included, ranged from $Ω(1)$ to $O(d\ln d)$, leaving even the scaling undetermined. We here prove that $Φ_{\rm p}(d)=Θ(d)$, and in particular that $\tfrac12\,d \le Φ_{\rm p}(d) \le 5\,d$ for all sufficiently large $d$. The upper bound counts hierarchical families of escape waypoints called tree embeddings; the lower bound is via a weighted second-moment estimate on an explicit ensemble of ballistic escape routes. A linear scaling of $Φ_{\rm p}(d)$ excludes the $d\ln d$ growth suggested by analogy with other systems in the random first-order transition universality class and is consistent with the numerical estimate $Φ_{\rm p}/d \to 3.40(5)$. Because the mean-field dynamical transition is likewise linear, $Φ_{\rm d}\simeq 2.40\,d$, our result fixes the activated window $[Φ_{\rm d},Φ_{\rm p}]$ as a bounded---rather than diverging---correction to mean-field dynamical arrest in sufficiently high $d$.

title: Anisotropic g-tensor and strong spin-orbit interaction of holes in hexagonal germanium nanowires
summary: Hexagonal germanium combines direct-gap optical activity with the low-nuclear-spin environment of a group-IV material, making it a candidate platform for spin qubits and spin-photon interfaces. Using a ten-band $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$ model, we study the response of confined hole states in hexagonal germanium nanowires to magnetic and electric fields. We show that, by symmetry, the top valence band of the bulk crystal has a vanishing $g$ factor in the plane perpendicular to the $c$ axis, in analogy with the in-plane $g$ factor of heavy holes in two-dimensional hole gases. In nanowires, confinement induces only small transverse $g$-tensor components, so the $g$ tensor remains strongly anisotropic. A transverse electric field strongly reduces the nanowire band gap, providing a gate-tunable optical signature and limiting the usable field range. The same field induces a Rashba spin-orbit interaction that is markedly stronger for fields perpendicular to the $c$ axis and depends nonlinearly on the field strength. In narrow wires at strong fields, the spin-orbit length reaches a few tens of nanometers, comparable to hole devices in cubic silicon. We identify the microscopic origin of the Rashba coupling as a second-order process mediated by a few intermediate subbands with distinct symmetry selection rules. Our results provide guidance for the design of electrically controlled hole-spin qubits in hexagonal germanium nanowires.

title: Contrasting fate of holes introduced by Fe or In in kagome metal CoSn
summary: CoSn is a kagome metal with well-defined flat bands 0.2 eV below the Fermi level EF. Moving them across EF would offer a rare opportunity to investigate their impact on electronic properties. Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and X-ray absorption at the Co K-edge, we examine two routes to introduce holes in this compound, through Co/Fe or Sn/In substitutions. Substituting In for Sn produces an almost rigid upward shift of the bands toward EF, as expected for hole doping, whereas substituting Fe for Co leads to an unexpected downward shift. Density functional theory calculations reproduce these opposite trends and trace the unusual behavior of Fe to its local magnetic moment. The moment keeps the hole on the Fe impurity and imposes an attractive electrostatic potential on neighboring Co atoms. Overall, both substitutions bring weakly dispersing states close to EF, the flat bands of the Co kagome lattice upon In substitution and partly localized states around magnetic Fe impurities upon Fe substitution.

title: Field-aligned measurement removes the anisotropy barrier of sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction
summary: Sample-based quantum subspace methods construct a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. We study these methods for heat conduction in magnetized plasmas, where the anisotropy $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp$ reaches $10^8$ to $10^{10}$. We prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. First, if the measurement basis is aligned with the flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by $\|r_0\|_{L^+}(χ_\parallel-χ_\perp)^{-1/2}$, where the numerator does not depend on $χ_\parallel$. The bound is sharp, so the accuracy improves as the anisotropy grows. Second, in the computational basis, a subspace that misses a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as $χ_\parallel^{-1/2}$, which gives an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. We verify both results on a shaped cross-section and on a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits. At $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp=10^9$, the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives $1.3\times10^{-5}$. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of $7.0\times10^{-6}$ with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to $1.2\times10^4$ shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.

title: Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable
summary: The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.

title: When Molecular Dimerization Induces Magnetic Bi-Stability at the Metal-Organic Interface
summary: We present a method to create metal-organic dimer complexes by on-surface assembly on a metal substrate using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS). We demonstrate that a dimer of Mn-Phthalocyanine (MnPc)2 on a Ag(111) surface can be switched between two stable configurations upon a small conformational change controlled by STM manipulation. By means of density-functional theory calculations, it is found that the two conformations correspond to an antiferromagnetic (AFM) and a ferromagnetic (FM) state respectively. Directly coordinated Mn atoms of the dimer lead to an AFM-coupling whereas indirectly coordinated (shifted) Mn atoms lead to a FM-coupling. Rarely seen in a molecular- dimers with transition-metal atoms, the FM-AFM-FM transition is thus readily on-surface accessible. Furthermore, the two configurations of the switch are easily identified by their Kondo states, opening interesting routes in terms of both, writing (FM versus AFM states) and reading. These results pave the experimental route toward dimer-based materials with complex magnetic structures of potential interest for application in spintronics, logics and computing.

title: Non-Perturbative Resolution of Luttinger's Theorem Violations in Strongly Correlated Systems
summary: Many-body physics faces an apparent paradox concerning violations of Luttinger's theorem in strongly correlated systems. The theorem relates the electron number to the Luttinger count -- the monodromy of the logarithm of the imaginary-frequency Green's function $G(iε)$ -- and, at finite magnetic field, connects the Hall conductivity to the magnetic-field derivative of the Luttinger count via the Streda formula. Here, we provide a non-perturbative solution to this paradox. We demonstrate that the reported violations of Luttinger's theorem do not require a breakdown of the skeleton diagram representation of physical quantities, thereby resolving a long-standing point of contention in many-body theory. Furthermore, we show that the Luttinger integral, which accounts for the mismatch between the particle number and the Luttinger count, is itself a genuine topological invariant directly tied to the Luttinger-Ward functional $Φ[G]$ rather than to the Green's function alone. We demonstrate that this invariant, like the monodromy of $\ln G(iε)$ itself, stems exclusively from the zero-frequency discontinuity of the Matsubara trajectory.

title: Dithered Belief Propagation for Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. In the proceedings of QCE 2026
summary: We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.

title: Observable-Based Learning of Effective Entanglement Hamiltonians
summary: Determining the entanglement Hamiltonian (EH) of an interacting quantum many-body system remains a fundamental challenge beyond special analytically tractable cases. Here we develop an observable-matching framework for learning effective EHs, which we demonstrate using response estimates from quantum Monte Carlo. As applications of this framework, we first calibrate the overall prefactor of the lattice Bisognano--Wichmann (LBW) construction using equal-time correlations and then learn spatially resolved couplings beyond its prescribed profile, without assuming a specific functional form for their spatial dependence. Trained solely on local correlations, the learned EHs reproduce benchmarked von Neumann and second Rényi entropies in $1$D and second Rényi entropies in $2$D. For a strong-bond cut associated with special surface criticality at the $(2+1)$D $O(3)$ Wilson--Fisher critical point, free-form learning outperforms the calibrated LBW ansatz in predicting the second Rényi entropy and reveals spatially nonuniform coupling renormalizations. Importantly, the learned EH also provides access to the von Neumann entropy in this setting, revealing a negative subleading correction and extending previous Rényi entropy findings to the von Neumann case. Directly evaluating the von Neumann entropy in such $(2+1)$D interacting quantum many-body systems remains challenging for conventional numerical methods. These results establish observable-based learning as a route to constructing effective entanglement Hamiltonians beyond prescribed spatial profiles in higher-dimensional interacting systems.

title: Dynamical Keldysh model for colored noise and finite relaxation rate
summary: The Keldysh model describes quantum dots subjected to Gaussian noise with infinite correlation time. For multi-component noise coupled through non-commuting matrices, the spectrum exhibits a pseudogap. We solve the model for coloured noise with any correlation time, $1/ γ$. Finite memory leads to the pseudogap being filled, its peaks merging and the line narrowing.

title: Key role of orbital exchange in CoO magnetism
summary: Co ions in the antiferromagnetic phase of CoO are known to possess a substantial orbital moment, making this material promising for orbitronic applications. However, intersite exchange interactions involving these orbital degrees of freedom remain poorly quantified, and their role in CoO magnetism is unclear. Here, we derive a full low-energy effective Hamiltonian for CoO, including orbital exchange terms, using an ab initio force-theorem approach based on DFT+dynamical mean-field theory. We find sizable orbital interactions, with quadrupolar orbital exchange emerging as the dominant nearest-neighbor term. The collinear antiferromagnetic order obtained from the effective Hamiltonian features magnetic moments tilted away from the pseudocubic <001> direction and an orbital contribution amounting to about one-third of the total moment, in agreement with experimental estimates. We show that the moment tilting originates from the combined effect of orbital and spin-orbital exchange interactions. The same interactions also produce a prominent splitting of the lowest excitation band. By directly modeling the inelastic neutron scattering (INS) intensity, we further show that the characteristic column-like structures previously observed in CoO INS provide a clear fingerprint of orbital exchange. We also discuss possible impact of our findings for further advances in the field of complex collective excitations, their transport properties and applications in the realm of orbitronics.

title: Improving Gravitationally Induced Entanglement in Interferometric Configurations
summary: Proposals to detect gravitationally induced entanglement between massive particles offer a promising pathway toward probing the quantum nature of gravity. We perform a systematic geometric optimization and comparative analysis of Stern--Gerlach (SG) and Mach--Zehnder (MZ) matter-wave interferometers for this purpose, deriving exact analytical expressions for the gravitational phase of each configuration. Our first key result is that geometric optimization is indispensable. For commonly assumed experimental parameters, neglecting the optimization of geometric ratios can suppress the accumulated phase, and hence the detectability of entanglement, by up to several orders of magnitude. Second, we provide a complete comparative analysis of two SG orientations (linear and parallel) and three MZ orientations (translation-symmetric, mirror-symmetric, and parallel-arms). The parallel-arms SG and MZ configurations tend to yield the largest phase accumulations and are nearly equivalent in performance, whereas the translation-symmetric MZ setup exhibits destructive-interference nulls that act as blind operating points where detection becomes ineffective. These observations highlight the importance of geometry-aware design. A Monte Carlo error analysis of realistic fabrication tolerances indicates that the parallel-arms configurations are generally more robust, maintaining low relative phase uncertainty over broad parameter intervals. Furthermore, an evaluation of Bell violations assesses the feasibility and signal-to-noise ratio of each configuration. Our results identify geometric optimization, particularly through parallel-arms designs, as an important consideration for near-term experiments targeting gravitationally induced entanglement.

title: Extensions of the Haldane gap proof: higher dimensions, near degeneracy, fermions and tensor-network states
summary: A recent remarkable paper by OpenAI showed that the spin-one Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit. The proof elegantly deduces this gap from the Hamiltonian's spectrum on a finite system. This basic idea is an inequality involving the purity of the original Gibbs state and a dual Gibbs state that is defined via space-time rotation. Here we consider a few generalizations of this purity bootstrap argument. We first extend it to arbitrary spatial dimensions. Our main result uses the space-time duality between symmetry generators and symmetry twists to obtain upper bounds on the splitting of nearly degenerate low-energy states, together with a nonzero gap above them, from finite-system information. As applications, we show that finite-system calculations for the 2+1-D toric code in a field and the 2+1-D transverse-field Ising model establish parameter regimes with four and two low-lying states whose splittings are bounded from above by $e^{-cL}$ and $e^{-cL^2}$ respectively for arbitrarily large system size $L$, while the gap above these states remains nonzero in the thermodynamic limit. Next, we extend it to fermionic systems and use a finite calculation to establish a symmetric mass generation phase in a $2+1$-D fermionic model. Finally, we apply the bootstrap to tensor-network states and establish exponential decay of connected correlations of all local operators in the symmetric square-lattice spin-one state introduced by Jian and Zaletel.

title: Anisotropy lifts topological protection of transport in pumped spin chains
summary: We investigate the prospect of topological spin pumping and transport in a dimerized spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ anisotropic XY chain with tunable in-plane anisotropy. Through a Jordan-Wigner transformation, the system maps onto an extended Rice-Mele-type fermionic model whose momentum-space band structure exhibits gapped regions characterized by nonzero Chern numbers ($\pm 1$) as well as trivial and gapless regimes. Conventional momentum-space analysis therefore predicts quantized Thouless-type spin pumping in parts of the Chern number diagram. However, real-space time evolution under open boundary conditions reveals that the spin transport is generally not quantized away from the isotropic limit. In the anisotropic regime, eigen-energy states within the transporting subspace hybridize during the driving cycle, leading to a transport that depends on details of the driving protocol. Quantized pumping and transport survive only in the isotropic limit, where the Hamiltonian reduces to decoupled Rice-Mele sectors and the transported spin component is conserved. Our results demonstrate that momentum-space topological invariants alone do not guarantee quantized spin transport in anisotropic spin chains. More broadly, they show that the conventional Thouless-pumping framework does not straightforwardly extend to situations where the transported quantity is not conserved, highlighting the importance of real-space diagnostics in topological transport phenomena.

title: Spin supersolid in triangular lattice easy-axis spin-1/2 antiferromagnet: a fermionic parton perspective
summary: We study the supersolid order of the spin-1/2 easy-axis XXZ antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice using a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the $π$-flux Dirac spin liquid, with the mean-field order generated by an on-site spinon interaction term and nearest-neighbor (anisotropic) spin couplings. The collective modes are obtained using the random-phase approximation (RPA). In a finite parameter region, we find the Y state as a self-consistent solution, together with the competing Y' state, which is a $90^\circ$-rotated Y state inside the order plane. The mean-field energy favors Y', even though the two states are exactly degenerate in the classical limit. However, the Y state can become lower in energy when higher-order corrections due to the fluctuations of the collective modes are considered. The Y state can also be stabilized on the mean-field level by applying small external fields, which we do in two different ways: moment-aligned local field and uniform field along the easy axis. In both cases, the RPA calculation for the stabilized Y state gives a roton minimum at the $M$ point in the excitation spectrum. A gapped pseudo-Goldstone mode above the gapless Goldstone mode is obtained as well, which has also been observed experimentally. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of tuning the spinon interaction strength and the anisotropy in spin couplings in our phenomenological model. Comparison with the recent numerical and experimental results is also discussed.

title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
summary: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.

title: Initial heat-current decay versus thermal transport at a three-body resonance in a one-dimensional Fermi gas
summary: We theoretically study kinetic relaxation and heat transport in a dilute one-dimensional spinless Fermi gas near a three-body resonance. The full vacuum amplitude of a finite-range interaction enters the linearized Boltzmann collision operator. The resonance position that maximizes the initial heat-current decay rate lies above the one that minimizes the integrated relaxation time. At higher resonance energies, coupling among momentum moments transfers heat-current weight to a slow mode. A faster initial decay can therefore coexist with slower subsequent relaxation and a larger low-frequency heat response. The dissipative responses at two resonance positions reverse their ordering at least twice as frequency increases. Bounds on the full collision operator confirm both reversals. A fourth-moment distortion exhibits the same separation of relaxation scales and provides a probe through the momentum distribution.

title: Synaptic Multi-Weight Wafer-Scale Domain Wall Magnetic Tunnel Junctions Driven by Spin Orbit Torque
summary: Spintronic synaptic devices based on magnetic random access memory (MRAM) are a rapidly evolving class within the analog neuromorphic architecture. However, obtaining the multi-weight or analog behavior desired for improved neural network inference accuracy in scaled MRAM remains a challenge. In this study, we demonstrate and tune up to eight distinct resistance levels in 300 mm wafer-scale magnetic tunnel junction artificial synapses driven by spin orbit torque. By varying the applied in-plane field, multi-weight resistance states emerge through domain wall nucleation and pinning. These multi-weight states appear stochastically and can be addressed with an iterative programming algorithm to program a specific resistance. Electromagnetic simulations indicate the multiple states are due to domain wall nucleation mediated by in-plane field and applied voltage. Implementation of the measured multi-weight devices in a neural network yields a 96.1% inference accuracy using the MNIST dataset if all devices provide the same number of multi-weight states. When experimental device-to-device variation is included, the accuracy is 48.6%. Overall, this work demonstrates a route towards multi-weight artificial synapse MRAM, establishing a path towards scalable neuromorphic systems based on spintronics.

title: Multimagnon bound states in the polarized phase of anisotropic antiferromagnets
summary: We investigate single-ion bound magnon states in the high-field polarized phase of uniaxial antiferromagnets. By solving the two-particle problem exactly, we determine the dispersion of bound magnon pairs both below and above the continuum. We also obtain rigorous bounds on their binding energies by using the Gershgorin circle theorem. For spin-1 easy-axis systems, two-magnon bound states with zero total momentum emerge as low-energy excitations once the ratio of single-ion anisotropy to exchange exceeds a threshold value. As the field decreases, magnon pairs condense, driving a transition into a spin-nematic phase. Beyond the two-magnon problem, we develop a general strong-coupling approach that describes $n$-magnon single-ion bound states ($n\leq 2S$) in large-$S$ easy-axis antiferromagnets. The Bose-Einstein condensation of these multi-magnon excitations yields a rich hierarchy of field-induced multipolar phases stabilized by single-ion anisotropy. Comparisons with recent experiments on Na$_2$BaNi(PO$_4$)$_2$ and Sr$_2$CoGe$_2$O$_7$ illustrate the quantitative power of our theory.

title: Thermally-driven quantum reservoir computing
summary: Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

title: FNO-Based Inverse Co-Design of Semiconducting Quantum-Dot Devices
summary: Gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots are promising building blocks for scalable spin-based quantum processors, however their operational properties depend on several fabrication and control parameters, such as lithographic gate layout and applied voltages. Existing device architectures have been refined through repeated fabrication and experimental testing, producing layouts that support reliable device operation. However, this process does not exhaustively explore the design space, limiting the ability to obtain qubits with targeted properties. We address these challenges by presenting a differentiable inverse co-design framework for electrostatically defined quantum dots that jointly optimises gate voltages and the gate electrode layout. A semiclassical Thomas--Fermi electrostatic simulator provides reference data for a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate, which predicts the two-dimensional charge-density field. The desired spatial distribution of the confined charge defines the target quantum-dot geometry for inverse design. The FNO reproduces charge densities with a relative $L^2$ test error of just 0.6\% and enables millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations. Relative to the CPU-based physics simulator, the FNO achieves a 17,000-fold speed-up on GPU for a single design, with further performance gains enabled by batched inference. When embedded in a gradient-based design loop with fabrication constraints, the FNO can produce both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions. The ability to engineer these distinct confinement configurations demonstrates control over quantum-dot shape and position, providing a route towards designing devices with distinct qubit-relevant operating properties prior to fabrication.

title: Direct transition from a fractional Chern insulator to a topological superconductor
summary: We find numerical evidence for a direct continuous transition from a Laughlin fractional Chern insulator (FCI) to a $c_-=3/2$ topological superconductor (TSC), driven by increasing bandwidth at filling $ν=1/3$ in a repulsively interacting Chern band. At the critical point, the electron correlation length diverges at momentum away from the reference Fermi surface. We develop a generalized theory of superconducting-vortex proliferation for this transition. Magnetic translation organizes the vortices into six valleys, so translation-preserving proliferation requires additional gauge fields. The resulting theory reproduces the momentum structure of the critical spectrum and captures the divergent electron correlation. Upon doping away from commensurate filling, the theory gives rise to a superconducting dome. These results are consistent with an anyonic origin of the topological superconductivity in the absence of a weak-coupling Fermi-surface instability.

title: Upper and lower bounds for few-copy Gaussian tomography, and the absence of a fermionic warm regime
comment: 32 pages, 2 tables. Extends arXiv:2609.23189 to measurements on blocks of k copies; uses Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.26705 as a black box
summary: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill proved a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states need $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies under single-copy or few-copy measurements, warm ones $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$. The author proved $Ω(m^3/ε^2)$ for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. This note shows the crossover has no fermionic counterpart and extends the fermionic bound to blocks of $k$ copies. There is no warm regime: on the quadratic Gibbs balls $β\|h\|_F\leβ_0$ of unknown Hamiltonian $h$, the single-copy rate is $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ for every fixed $β_0>0$, at accuracies that resolve the ball, with a lower-bound constant independent of $β_0$. At the maximally mixed state a replicated-parameter Fisher budget gives $N>m^3/(8{,}553{,}600\,k\,ε^2)$ for blocks of at most $k$ copies and all $ε\le1/3600$; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information, via spinor tensor powers of $\mathfrak{so}(2m)$, shows that the budget $mt^2$ behind it is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size; whether $1/k$ is the true rate is open. Near the vacuum, block protocols need $Ω(m^3/(ε^2\min\{\sqrt k,m\}))$ copies, with no logarithm, via an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography; parity superselection changes no rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. The embedding also carries upper bounds: a particle-number measurement followed by the $k$-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every $k$ on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number, and a heterodyne stage that undoes displacement and squeezing extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states. This closes their $k$-entangled gap on the cold class; intermediate temperatures remain open.

title: Ground-State Dressing and Delayed Feedback of a Chiral Giant Atom in Ultrastrong Waveguide QED
summary: We study a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. At a relative coupling phase π/2, the total spectral density is independent of the distance between the coupling points, whereas its directional components are not. Using a variational polaron transformation, we show that the renormalized transition frequency and the total ground-state dressing inherit this independence, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. A sudden switch-off of the coupling releases this cloud as directional radiation. We also derive the spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, showing that, after neglecting the local photonic potential, the memory kernel becomes distance independent at the same phase.

title: Threshold-Free Symmetry-Enriched Topological Quantum Memory
summary: We show that non-Abelian symmetry enrichment can protect a toric code memory against incoherent electric noise at any bond error probability $p\in[0,1]$. For a toric code on the honeycomb lattice coupled to $Sp(N)$ rotors, with electric anyons carrying the fundamental representation, we construct an efficient minimum-weight decoder whose logical error probability decays exponentially with system size for $N\ge40$, a conservative sufficient bound. The same decoder also rules out strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking in the fundamental channel of $Sp(N)$ under the corresponding local decoherence in two dimensions. The construction extends to other symmetries, including $SU(N)$.

title: Unifying First-Order Coherence, Concurrence, and Bell Correlations in Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
summary: Neutrino oscillations provide a natural setting for investigating the quantum character of flavor conversion and the distribution of quantum resources over macroscopic distances. Here, we study exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value in coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations. By expressing the evolving neutrino as a three-qubit single-excitation state, we derive the generally mixed two-qubit reductions and show that the squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode and its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity. Furthermore, a closed two-branch relation is obtained, showing that the maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair is determined by its average first-order coherence and concurrence. The branch structure follows from the correlation-tensor spectrum and yields exact conditions for CHSH violation. For the vacuum parameters and propagation ranges considered, electron preparation gives weak CHSH violations in electroncontaining pairs, while muon preparation produces a dominant utau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations. The comparison also identifies the thirdflavor contribution responsible for the different locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima. These results clarify the distribution of quantum correlations during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extensions to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

title: Higher-order topological quantum battery
summary: A quantum battery is a next-generation energy-storage device that exploits genuinely quantum properties such as superposition and coherence. We propose a second-order topological quantum battery coupled to a photonic crystal described by the breathing-Kagome model, where optical loss is present on all lattice sites while nonlinear gains are introduced selectively at the output sites. Under these realistic non-Hermitian conditions, the system exhibits a clear topological phase transition manifested in both the ergotropy and the charging power. Remarkably, perfect work extraction is realized in the topological phase, where the maximum value of the ergotropy is quantized and acts as a good topological-phase indicator. The triangular geometry coherently distributes energy into two quantum batteries, where mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization gives rise to collective energy storage.

title: Single-shot ground-state preparation via strongly coupled baths
summary: Preparing ground and thermal states of quantum many-body systems is a central task in quantum simulation. Dissipative protocols have emerged as a promising solution for both near-term and fault-tolerant hardware, but most constructions rely on weak system-bath coupling, leading to slow cooling. Here, we construct cooling protocols at strong system-bath coupling, and demonstrate accurate state preparation within even a single cooling cycle. Our protocols combine dynamically ramped ancilla energy levels with time-dependent couplings to optimize the trade-off between cooling error and physical time. For a general class of free-fermion systems, we reduce the dynamics exactly to a two-level scattering problem: ground-state cooling becomes a control problem of maximizing resonant excitation transfer while suppressing non-adiabatic heating. We then construct a family of ``Möbius-Ingham'' protocols, which reach optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of the leading heating error for gapped spectra, as a function of the cycle period. In our free-fermion benchmarks, Möbius-Ingham cooling lies on the Pareto frontier between steady-state error and cooling time among the controls tested. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in interacting Ising and $t$-$V$ chains and the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Finally, we extend our construction to Gibbs state preparation, showing how free-fermion thermal states can be prepared in a single cycle.

title: Quantum simulation of classical RCL circuits via complexification and Schrödingerization
summary: The decomplexification procedure establishes a mathematical equivalence between finite dimensional quantum dynamics and classical dynamics by mapping the complex quantum domain onto the real classical one. Its inverse process, complexification --- which lifts a classical dynamics to an equivalent quantum formulation --- is of great interest, particularly because it enables the quantum simulation of equations that are of classical relevance. In this way, one can prepare the solution of classical differential equations to be implemented using quantum computation tools. In the present work, we recall the decomplexification procedure and also discuss several distinct strategies for performing the complexification of classical equations, so as to obtain the corresponding quantum-equivalent dynamics.

title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection
summary: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.

title: Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable
summary: The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.
